items.title: Book Review: Broken Money and the Way Out, PART 1: MONEY (the Invity Team)
items.text:
TAKEAWAY NUMERO UNO: If there's a successful book titled *Broken Money*, you DO NOT title your own marketing pamphlet/e-book style "Broken Money" as well.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159635)

***

I spent some time today looking through the Invity people's fintech offering. We met at BTCHEL, where they launched/announced some cool banking features for us Europooreans. https://stacker.news/items/1580878, https://stacker.news/items/1581849 https://stacker.news/items/1585380

Particularly, quite convenient **auto-stacking, payment cards with bitcoin/stablecoins,** and **juicy-af cashback** on every spend. (Up to stupidly [low maximums](https://www.invity.io/personal-accounts), it turns out -.-)

This is all very tempting, and Den is a sucker for a good sats deal (*aren't we all?!*), so what does a bookish nerd do?

## Download and read the free e-book, of course!

***

It's from their educational platform, Invity Academy (as if we didn't have enough educational outlets...):

> It is meant for people who know Bitcoin from headlines and debates, but never got an answer to the most important question: why did it come about at all, and what problem does it solve?
> We start with money itself — how it came about, how it works today, and why so many people feel that something about it „broke“. Only once we understand the problem does it make sense to talk about a solution.

Oh, turns out this is *really* for Mr. Den. Let's dig in.

*Blah-blah-blah*, money's three functions, and various properties (ignoring, for now, Erik Yakes' *7th Property*, **Immutability** https://stacker.news/items/1572208)

![](https://m.stacker.news/159636)

...gold, commodity money, stock-to-flows. Alright, amazing. State intervention, Roman coins.

## "If you were born after 1971, you live in a historical anomaly"

Pretty neat account:

* 1870-1914: Classical gold standard
* 1933: gold banned
* 1971 Nixon Shock

They definitely overdo the importance of 1971, a mere formality in a world already addicted to fiat and money printing. (1914 is a more important civilizational cutoff.)

Cool, but graphs like these are pretty boring. A *dollar*, like *a* bitcoin, is not a meaningful economic unit; nobody (rationally) cares about *a* dollar, but the relationship between what they have and earn to what they invest and consume. e.g., https://stacker.news/items/737272, https://stacker.news/items/1578595

![](https://m.stacker.news/159637)

> 1913 the Fed, 1933 the ban on holding gold, 1944 Bretton Woods, 1971 the Nixon Shock — four steps from hard money to fiat. → Since 1971 no currency in the world has been backed by anything tangible

VERY nice

![](https://m.stacker.news/159638)

> How money is actually created today
> → The vast majority of the money in your account was created by commercial banks, not the state.
> → New money comes into being at the moment of a loan. When you repay the loan, the money disappears.
> → QE lets a central bank create money in the order of trillions within weeks.
> → The M2 money supply grows substantially faster than real output.

## AMAZINGLY witty: "Money-supply inflation is the cause, price inflation is the symptom."

![](https://m.stacker.news/159639)

Here's a scary graph, but of course *financing conditions* matters too: An average interest rate for mortgages in Czechia was about [7% in 2000](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Average-mortgage-loan-interest-rate-1995-2005_fig7_24080862); [below 5%](https://www.globalpropertyguide.com/europe/czech-republic/mortgage-interest-rate) in 2025.

## Inflation as a silent tax

![](https://m.stacker.news/159641)

> Modern central banking is often defended with the argument that it stimulates the economy and creates jobs. Even if we take that at face value, we must at the same time see the flip side: the money a central bank creates does not arrive for everyone at once. It travels a predictable path that structurally favours one group over another.

VERY eloquent and punchy.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159640)

> At the end of the pipe stand

* **The fixed-wage employee**: the wage is usually adjusted only with a delay, and not by the full extent of inflation.
* **The pensioner** — the pension is indexed once a year, slowly.
* **The young family** without assets — they own no assets to rise in value, yet pay higher prices for food, energy, rent.
  -**The saver** on a savings account — the interest does not cover the loss of purchasing power

These things are conditional and not *obviously* and *always* the case; boomers in America enjoy pretty competitive COLAs; interest rates on savings accounts in Iceland are ~halfway between CPI and monetary expansion. With bond prices collapsing, rates on (high-yield, short-term) bank accounts like those at fintechs are bound to rise explosively. https://stacker.news/items/1578425

***

## NOTHING STOPS THIS LYN ALDEN TRAIN

Yeah, dudes didn't just *borrow* Lyn's title; they take her fiscal framework too: there's no way back/out from governments' profligacy and debt-to-GDP ratios. America just *cannot* outgrow [40trn in debt](https://stacker.news/items/1554591) (...unless we scalp the boomers https://stacker.news/items/1468968, you know the drill.)

> An economic term returning to the debate in recent years is fiscal dominance. It means a state of affairs where the state’s budgetary situation is so strained that the central bank cannot run an independent policy. Lyn Alden describes that the United States entered this situation around 2022. The interest cost on US federal debt exceeded the defence budget in 2024 — and that is a defence budget which is itself larger than the budgets of the next ten largest countries combined.

The financial FIXES that used to work:

* The **60/40 portfolio**: yeah, it's entirely dead. Also, bonds don't provide *neither* uncorrelated returns, nor inflation-adjusted returns at all.
* savings account: guaranteed losses. Czech republic example is \~4% interest on savings, 2.5% official inflation... BUT tax the nominal return 15% *and* assets like flats and properties rose *way more* than 1-2%.
* New fixes?

> Holding large cash in the bank is, over the long run, a strategy by which the state really taxes your purchasing power. Diversification remains valuable, but it must include assets that respond to monetary degradation (hard assets). Gold passed the test of 5,000 years. Neutral, apolitical, independent of the banking system. Bitcoin is new — it has 15 years behind it. But if its properties are confirmed, it offers everything gold does, and more: portability, verifiability, divisibility and neutrality in a form gold can never have.

...in PART 2, dudes move on to the orange solution: \_bitcoin\_, woop woop!

items.title: It's Ghey To Care About Climate Change (FT, Pilita Clark)
items.text:
Yeah, we all know the reason climate change ~~activism~~ delusion doesn't have a higher uptick is... *toxic masculinity*!

**oh lord.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/160711)

> **If you are a man who cares about climate change, are you a bit of a dweeb? Put another way, if a man says global warming is rubbish, does he seem more manly**? In my 15 years of writing about climate change, these are not questions I have considered before. But I have begun to do so since coming across research that suggests a lot of men brush off the climate problem for fear of seeming too feminine.

## why do studies and polls across the world consistently show that men care less about global warming than women?

It's all just socialization and sexism.

> Some studies suggest that men feel they have more to lose from policies to fight climate change. Others conclude it is because women are socialised to care more about things like the environment. But researchers who focus on socialisation tend to look at it from the perspective of the women being socialised.

*alternative candidates*: women constitutionally less fit for public convos (unlikely), women too high in neuroticism/liable to catastrophizing (plausible), women harder time thinking through trade-offs/op cost (maybe); men more attuned to the real professions that make society function (definitely).

> Using data from the US, and a long-running survey of more than 40,000 people across Europe, he showed that men who say they want to save the planet are perceived to be more warm and caring. In keeping with this finding, he also showed that men who are strongly concerned about maintaining their sense of manhood express less concern about the climate problem and say they feel less responsibility for managing it.

## GIEF MANHOOD!

> A study of more than 9,000 scientists in 115 countries published this week shows that those who believe technology will largely solve the climate problem are 23 per cent less likely to go on a climate march, sign a petition or take similar civic actions, compared with scientists who lack such faith. The techno-optimists are also 18 per cent less likely to make big lifestyle changes to cut carbon. In other words, many personal views matter, even for experts.

Being attuned to tech (fixed) make you less activist-worthy... sooo, having a male-oriented mind must be bad/sexist.

## "But Haselhuhn’s work does raise a question about the best way to sell the need for climate action, especially to men."

lol, yeah... because it's all a matter of *marketing*. No substance problem, no economic consideration, no green-stuff-was-just-low-interest-rate-phenomenon.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160712)

oh, and just FYI... if you object to climate "facts," you're not just in denial: **you're suffering from SOLUTION AVERSION.** *Fucksake, give me a break*.

> It doesn’t help to spout scientific facts to show why \[your climate-denying uncle, a man\*\*] is wrong, Hayhoe told a recent FT conference. That’s because the real issue here is not science denial but solution aversion, or concern that climate policies will clash with a person’s identity, ideology or ideas about a better world.

> **Because it’s unpleasant to say openly that you don’t want to fix a serious problem, people use so-called motivated reasoning to find grounds** for why climate change cannot be real or serious. In other words, they process information in ways that align with what they already believe or want, rather than with objective evidence.

Or... maybe, just *maybe*, there's a deeper, higher-order, system-levels thinking required... trading off one thing for another, or (peeeerhaps??) it's not as bad as the green activists \~say\~ scream loudly on the tube, covered in pig's blood...

Ah fuck. Some people's (dare I say, *women?!*) intellectual echo chambers and cognitive deficiencies are, eh, shocking.

> Happily, Hayhoe says, the same uncle’s views can reverse completely if he buys solar panels that save him money or does something else that improves his own circumstances as well as the climate. There is a message here for **those of us who rightly worry about warming temperatures.** Scientific facts really matter, as does the health of the environment. But there will be times when the best thing you can do for the planet is not talk about it at all.

DEFINITELY a candidate for the stupidest thing I read this week.

# The middle child of my Woody propaganda series

![](https://m.stacker.news/162686)

The [Guitaxe](https://stacker.news/items/1596515) got another big brother. While the little guy is great for learning, and his biggest brother hashes like a beast, the s9 version has a special super power. This space heater not only kills fascists, it's moving into my neighbor's garage. She's "always cold" and I'm always trying to foist my hashrate's power consumption on other people. It's a match made in heaven. Woot! This is my first American home mining deploy.

This got me thinking, how many garages will it take?

# [Hashrate Hearth](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162687)

Foundry and the AntPool mafia currently build **58%** of bitcoin's block templates. My new site explores how much home mining it will take to break that majority, and different ways we can get there.

# The Skinny

First, you pick a goal and one machine and a gauge shows how many homes it takes to reach said goal. As of this writing, breaking the aforementioned majority takes **160 EH/s** of new hashrate. That's **800k homes with an S21**, 1.5 million with a used S19j Pro, 12 million with an S9... or **133 million with a Bitaxe**. Only about 106 million people currently own bitcoin directly. There's also a slider for how much of that home fleet ends up in the US, because China's 2021 ban showed where the hashrate sits is relevant too.

You can flip the chart between coinbase tags and who builds the templates. By tag, it takes three pools to make a majority. But if you go by builder (b10c's research) it's two. A setup comparison shows who determines the transactions in each case.

Plug in your home scenario and you get a daily ledger. There are presets for winter heat on grid power, midday solar surplus, and hydronic heat + solar, plus credit to the folks boxing this stuff up for normal people like Canaan Avalon, Heatbit, Hashrate House and Exergy. (I believe that Heatbit is making a big announcement in about twenty minutes, btw)

I included a scenario to explore the hashrate exodus to AI. Props to @optimism for calling my attention to how this might actually create **more** consolidation though. Then I include some action steps, but if you read my posts regularly, there are no surprises there. :)

It has beautiful, sloppily vibe-coded ambience. Make sure to turn the sound **on**. You're welcome.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162694)

Plus, you don't get the steam effects when the sound is off. Those are the breaks.

# Why

Last week, @Scoresby asked me a question with presuppositions that grated pretty harshly with my experience in the last few years:

> What value do you see home miners bringing that industrial miners do not bring?

Around that same time, I had a call with a proprietary mining company about getting machines down to Mossel Bay. They were kind, generous people, not banal shitcoiners. Their advice, after hearing my whole rant on the value of decentralization and censorship resistance, was still to skip bitcoin and mine altcoins. They argued that home-friendly machines pay about the same and the pool converts payouts anyway. If Foundry and AntPool start with some funny business, they lose nothing. The family saving in bitcoin loses a ton.

So here's my answer. It's not the machine. It's which template is being hashed and who's holding the bitcoin. That's not charity. It's defending savings.

# And this morning's news makes it pretty timely!

The HRF newsletter this morning just reported that Russia has announced that after July 2027, self custody is [essentially banned for private citizens](https://cointelegraph.com/news/russia-ban-p2p-crypto-trades-july-2027). That's coming from the country hosting about a sixth of global hashrate. Currently, those kind of rules get enforced at exchanges. When somebody decides to enforce on-chain, won't the cheapest place to do it be the handful of pools that build most block templates?

# Prove me wrong (please!)

I'm still looking to lose this argument (that we have a mining pool centralization problem). In the meantime, let me know if your garage is getting chilly.

items.title: Why Are Bond Yields Suddenly so High?! (FT, Chris Giles)
items.text:
*Great question, few good answers.*

![](https://m.stacker.news/160553)

"The big question is why yields have risen so much."

* Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability?
* Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth?
* Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders?
* Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation?
* Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back?
* Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility?
* Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Chris Giles goes through some of these and provide some decent rebuttals.

> Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were [three broad reasons](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20260916.pdf) at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.
> The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

## "The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling"

![](https://m.stacker.news/160554)

Seems obvious, but I'm still a little stuck on the **transmission mechanism** : there's no reason, in principle, that wars or even oil price shocks ought to result in higher yields

The analogy being the 1970 had a few other critical components: **labor unions aggressively striking** for higher wages, setting off a price-wage push; and **central banks eager to accommodate** the real-cost push with new money.

There's no risk for the former, as labor unions worldwide (minus the Nordics, but they're pretty meek here) are a ghost of their former self. And the latter is entirely under our own control; central bankers can decide not to accommodate oil price increases (or actively crush demand... ), thus gaining credibility for their monetary policy *and* an indication of how independent they are from the fiscal authorities.

I guess, then, the bond market is pragmatic and saying "Fat chance, Den; dream the fuck on — dudes will print."

STILL, I find it kind of weird, then, to jump past the intermediate steps and conclude that wars (or oil prices) cause inflation and thus yields.  **No, (central) *banks printing money* cause inflation, *always and everywhere*.** For immediate analogy: Planes don't crash because of gravity, even though of course gravity is involved and 'ultimately' the cause.

> There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift.

Another commonly quipped reason is that AI has unleashed *massive* productivity gains that are about to swamp GDP numbers -- thus rates ought to go up (via the real economy). So far, only a single quarter of a sliver of such indications. AND:

> anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

Also, this investment boom is not *that* visible (outside specific sectors):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160560)

The other option is that capital is *expensive* now, with AI debt issuance swallowing up all the air in the room, *lol mixing metaphors*:

> Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

> there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros.

## "No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default."

eeeh, cute. *Maybe look further afield than your standard sources, fren*?!

***

Archive still messing w us... lmk if you want the full article -- lots of good graphs in there.

items.title: Bitcoin Activism (Not a Social Movement)
items.text: **TL;DR:** Here it is! My latest post on Bitcoin. I had this thought long ago, about four years ago, that Bitcoin could be a social movement. I mean, I studied social psychology so I saw some recurrent themes. Well, after four years, I now wrote it and added a lot to the list. Bitcoin is not a movement per se, but small micro-mobilisations that happen here and there, that just happen to use Bitcoin. items.text:
This is totally vibecoded, but the concept is interesting:

Run your wallet on hardware that was built before Bitcoin came out and that doesn't have wifi or bluetooth or a radio of any sort. Also it has a kind of nice plausible deniability to it.

> The private key is generated on the console from 128 coin flips you watch land, and it never leaves the cartridge. It signs its own spends: BIP-341 key-path taproot, BIP-340 Schnorr, computed on a 4 MHz 8-bit CPU, and the signed transaction leaves the console the only way anything can -- through the screen, as QR codes or as hex you can read.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162691)

It seems like you have to tell the signer about transactions you want to sign by hand:

> The coins you own are typed in by hand from a block explorer, because that is the only way facts about the chain can reach a machine with no antenna.

In general the flow is interesting:

|                                                                                                            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ![The professor](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/02-professor.png)             | **Talk to the professor.** Every line of dialogue, every screen and every character lives in [`content/story.txt`](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/blob/main/content/story.txt), not in the C.                        |
| ![Choosing a starter](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/03-starter.png)          | **Pick a starter.** Bitcoin is the only one that hatched in this world. The other two refuse to be selected.                                                                                                                  |
| ![Choosing an egg](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/04-egg.png)                 | **Pick an egg.** SWIFT is one standalone key, backed up as a WIF string, and hatches in about 70 seconds. ANCIENT is a 12-word BIP-39 seed phrase at `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0`, restorable in any wallet, and takes about 19 minutes. |
| ![Flipping coins for entropy](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/05-flipping.png) | **Flip your key.** One press, one coin flip, straight onto the grid. 128 flips, 128 bits. The counters show heads, tails and the longest run of the same result.                                                              |
| ![All 128 flips taken](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/06-flips-done.png)      | **Check the tally, then keep it.** 128 fair flips land near 64/64 with no run much past eight. `SELECT` throws the sequence away and starts again.                                                                            |
| ![Deriving the key](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/07-hatching.png)           | **Wait for the hatch.** The bar is driven from the VBlank interrupt, so the screen keeps moving while the CPU grinds through the elliptic curve.                                                                              |
| ![The wallet menu](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/09-wallet-menu.png)         | **The wallet.** Address, QR code, your UTXO list and balance, the secret, the raw output key, and save-to-cartridge.                                                                                                          |
| ![The taproot address](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/10-address.png)         | **A real `bc1p…` address.** 62 characters of bech32m over four lines.                                                                                                                                                         |
| ![The QR code](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/11-receive-qr.png)              | **Receive by QR.** Version 3, error-correction level L, 29×29 modules at three pixels each. A phone reads it straight off the screen.                                                                                         |
| ![The UTXO list](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/12-utxos.png)                 | **Your own ledger.** Transaction id, output index and amount, typed in from a block explorer, kept in cartridge SRAM with its own checksum.                                                                                   |

items.title: Pleb Economist #14: The Secretary Problem
items.text:
@denlillaapan mentioned [here](https://stacker.news/items/1598672/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1598713) that he'd be interested in seeing a writeup on what's known as the "Secretary Problem".  Turns out, it's been [discussed](https://stacker.news/items/933053/r/SimpleStacker) on SN before, and it's often sold as some "mathematical rule for life decisions".... but after studying up on it I think it's a *bit sillier and less applicable* than most people realize.  So here's my writeup on the subject.

The [Secretary Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_problem), as it's known, is a puzzle in probabilistic optimization theory.  Understanding the setup will help us understand how useful it is in real life.  The setup goes like this:

* You want to hire the best secretary out of N possible candidates.
* You don't know their quality levels until you interview them.
* You can only interview candidates one at a time.
* Once you interview a candidate, you gain sufficient information to rank them among all previously interviewed candidates, though you still don't know the rankings of the un-interviewed candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #1]` After you interview a candidate, you must immediately hire them or not... you can't wait to interview more candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #2]` If you reject them, you can't go back to them again later.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #3]` The only measure of success is hiring the *absolute best* out of the N candidates. Hiring the second best vs. hiring the third best are considered equal failures.

Note that since your only goal is to hire the absolute best, you'd only ever hire an interviewee if they're the best you've seen so far.  The basic tradeoff is this:

* If I hire them now, I risk the possibility that the best one would've come later.
* If I reject them now, I risk the possibility that they were actually the best.

The math is a bit tricky, but it turns out that the optimal decision rule is (approximately) to always reject the first 37% of candidates, then hire the first candidate afterwards who *ranks better than all the previous*.

The idea behind the solution is that it's too early to hire the first 37% you interview.  The probability that the best candidate is among the remaining applicants is still too high.  

### In popular media

The Secretary Problem has been used to describe search processes where you have to go through candidates one by one, like dating, house hunting, and job interviews.  It has achieved popular attention because of the seemingly ruthless rule of **automatically rejecting the first 37%**.  Especially when applied to dating, it would suggest that you should never marry your first few boyfriends/girlfriends, because *the probability that the best match is yet to come is still too high*.

### Critiques

The problem with applying this to real life is that some of the assumptions are unrealistic.  The worst culprit is `Unrealistic Assumption #3`.  The 37% rule is only optimal if you literally do not care about anything other than finding the *perfect match*.  The problem is set up in such a way that ending up with 2nd best is equally bad as ending up with the *worst candidate*.  There is no such scenario in real life where this is true, so the 37% rule is already not very applicable.

`Unrealistic Assumptions #1` and `#2` may be true in dating.  You often can't go back to a bf/gf that you've previously broken up with, and it's usually tough to explore multiple relationships at the same time.  However, in job interviews and house hunting, there are usually no such restrictions... there's just some risk that if you wait too long, the candidate is no longer available.  But that's a far cry from saying you have to immediately accept or reject a candidate after interviewing it.

One other thing I'll add is this.  The problem setup assumes you know what N is.  That is, you now exactly how many candidates there are going to be.  In most real life scenarios, like dating, you don't know that.  If you break up with your current partner, you don't know for sure another candidate is even going to arrive.

Oh, and one more unrealistic thing is that the information you get when you interview is purely *ordinal*, meaning it lets you *rank* the candidates, but it doesn't tell you an actual measure of the quality of *whether this person can do the job and how well*.  In most realistic settings, we care less about ranking amongst the candidates, and more about some absolute level of quality that we're looking for.

### Conclusion

It's a fun statistical puzzle, but the applicability to real life is way overstated.  One of those things where people hear a counterintuitive brutal strategy---"auTOmAtiCaLLy rEJECt thE FIrsT 37% oF APPLICanTs!"---and make much hay of it.... but yeah honestly you shouldn't do that in real life.

items.text:
<sub>TLDR: Check out </sub>[<sub>this site</sub>](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)<sub> that determines how much home mining it takes to dethrone the two companies that build most blocks. </sub>

[Hashrate Hearth](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)

# The middle child of my Woody propaganda series

![](https://m.stacker.news/162686)

The [Guitaxe](https://stacker.news/items/1596515) got another big brother. While the little guy is great for learning, and his biggest brother hashes like a beast, the s9 version has a special super power. This space heater not only kills fascists, it's moving into my neighbor's garage. She's "always cold" and I'm always trying to foist my hashrate's power consumption on other people. It's a match made in heaven. Woot! This is my first American home mining deploy.

This got me thinking, how many garages will it take?

# [Hashrate Hearth](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162687)

Foundry and the AntPool mafia currently build **58%** of bitcoin's block templates. My new site explores how much home mining it will take to break that majority, and different ways we can get there.

# The Skinny

First, you pick a goal and one machine and a gauge shows how many homes it takes to reach said goal. As of this writing, breaking the aforementioned majority takes **160 EH/s** of new hashrate. That's **800k homes with an S21**, 1.5 million with a used S19j Pro, 12 million with an S9... or **133 million with a Bitaxe**. Only about 106 million people currently own bitcoin directly. There's also a slider for how much of that home fleet ends up in the US, because China's 2021 ban showed where the hashrate sits is relevant too.

You can flip the chart between coinbase tags and who builds the templates. By tag, it takes three pools to make a majority. But if you go by builder (b10c's research) it's two. A setup comparison shows who determines the transactions in each case.

Plug in your home scenario and you get a daily ledger. There are presets for winter heat on grid power, midday solar surplus, and hydronic heat + solar, plus credit to the folks boxing this stuff up for normal people like Canaan Avalon, Heatbit, Hashrate House and Exergy. (I believe that Heatbit is making a big announcement in about twenty minutes, btw)

I included a scenario to explore the hashrate exodus to AI. Props to @optimism for calling my attention to how this might actually create **more** consolidation though. Then I include some action steps, but if you read my posts regularly, there are no surprises there. :)

It has beautiful, sloppily vibe-coded ambience. Make sure to turn the sound **on**. You're welcome.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162694)

Plus, you don't get the steam effects when the sound is off. Those are the breaks.

# Why

Last week, @Scoresby asked me a question with presuppositions that grated pretty harshly with my experience in the last few years:

> What value do you see home miners bringing that industrial miners do not bring?

Around that same time, I had a call with a proprietary mining company about getting machines down to Mossel Bay. They were kind, generous people, not banal shitcoiners. Their advice, after hearing my whole rant on the value of decentralization and censorship resistance, was still to skip bitcoin and mine altcoins. They argued that home-friendly machines pay about the same and the pool converts payouts anyway. If Foundry and AntPool start with some funny business, they lose nothing. The family saving in bitcoin loses a ton.

So here's my answer. It's not the machine. It's which template is being hashed and who's holding the bitcoin. That's not charity. It's defending savings.

# And this morning's news makes it pretty timely!

The HRF newsletter this morning just reported that Russia has announced that after July 2027, self custody is [essentially banned for private citizens](https://cointelegraph.com/news/russia-ban-p2p-crypto-trades-july-2027). That's coming from the country hosting about a sixth of global hashrate. Currently, those kind of rules get enforced at exchanges. When somebody decides to enforce on-chain, won't the cheapest place to do it be the handful of pools that build most block templates?

# Prove me wrong (please!)

I'm still looking to lose this argument (that we have a mining pool centralization problem). In the meantime, let me know if your garage is getting chilly.

<sub>P.S. Russia announcement also inspired a whole new section in </sub>[<sub>bitcoinisforcriminals.com</sub>](https://bitcoinisforcriminals.com)<sub>. Updating it now.</sub>

Off-wallet: opensource hardware wallet for Gameboy Color
items.text:
This is totally vibecoded, but the concept is interesting:

Run your wallet on hardware that was built before Bitcoin came out and that doesn't have wifi or bluetooth or a radio of any sort. Also it has a kind of nice plausible deniability to it.

> The private key is generated on the console from 128 coin flips you watch land, and it never leaves the cartridge. It signs its own spends: BIP-341 key-path taproot, BIP-340 Schnorr, computed on a 4 MHz 8-bit CPU, and the signed transaction leaves the console the only way anything can -- through the screen, as QR codes or as hex you can read.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162691)

It seems like you have to tell the signer about transactions you want to sign by hand:

> The coins you own are typed in by hand from a block explorer, because that is the only way facts about the chain can reach a machine with no antenna.

In general the flow is interesting:

|                                                                                                            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ![The professor](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/02-professor.png)             | **Talk to the professor.** Every line of dialogue, every screen and every character lives in [`content/story.txt`](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/blob/main/content/story.txt), not in the C.                        |
| ![Choosing a starter](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/03-starter.png)          | **Pick a starter.** Bitcoin is the only one that hatched in this world. The other two refuse to be selected.                                                                                                                  |
| ![Choosing an egg](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/04-egg.png)                 | **Pick an egg.** SWIFT is one standalone key, backed up as a WIF string, and hatches in about 70 seconds. ANCIENT is a 12-word BIP-39 seed phrase at `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0`, restorable in any wallet, and takes about 19 minutes. |
| ![Flipping coins for entropy](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/05-flipping.png) | **Flip your key.** One press, one coin flip, straight onto the grid. 128 flips, 128 bits. The counters show heads, tails and the longest run of the same result.                                                              |
| ![All 128 flips taken](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/06-flips-done.png)      | **Check the tally, then keep it.** 128 fair flips land near 64/64 with no run much past eight. `SELECT` throws the sequence away and starts again.                                                                            |
| ![Deriving the key](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/07-hatching.png)           | **Wait for the hatch.** The bar is driven from the VBlank interrupt, so the screen keeps moving while the CPU grinds through the elliptic curve.                                                                              |
| ![The wallet menu](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/09-wallet-menu.png)         | **The wallet.** Address, QR code, your UTXO list and balance, the secret, the raw output key, and save-to-cartridge.                                                                                                          |
| ![The taproot address](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/10-address.png)         | **A real `bc1p…` address.** 62 characters of bech32m over four lines.                                                                                                                                                         |
| ![The QR code](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/11-receive-qr.png)              | **Receive by QR.** Version 3, error-correction level L, 29×29 modules at three pixels each. A phone reads it straight off the screen.                                                                                         |
| ![The UTXO list](https://github.com/elRaulito/Off-wallet/raw/main/docs/shots/12-utxos.png)                 | **Your own ledger.** Transaction id, output index and amount, typed in from a block explorer, kept in cartridge SRAM with its own checksum.                                                                                   |

items.title: Pleb Economist #14: The Secretary Problem
items.text:
@denlillaapan mentioned [here](https://stacker.news/items/1598672/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1598713) that he'd be interested in seeing a writeup on what's known as the "Secretary Problem".  Turns out, it's been [discussed](https://stacker.news/items/933053/r/SimpleStacker) on SN before, and it's often sold as some "mathematical rule for life decisions".... but after studying up on it I think it's a *bit sillier and less applicable* than most people realize.  So here's my writeup on the subject.

The [Secretary Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_problem), as it's known, is a puzzle in probabilistic optimization theory.  Understanding the setup will help us understand how useful it is in real life.  The setup goes like this:

* You want to hire the best secretary out of N possible candidates.
* You don't know their quality levels until you interview them.
* You can only interview candidates one at a time.
* Once you interview a candidate, you gain sufficient information to rank them among all previously interviewed candidates, though you still don't know the rankings of the un-interviewed candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #1]` After you interview a candidate, you must immediately hire them or not... you can't wait to interview more candidates.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #2]` If you reject them, you can't go back to them again later.
* `[Unrealistic Assumption #3]` The only measure of success is hiring the *absolute best* out of the N candidates. Hiring the second best vs. hiring the third best are considered equal failures.

Note that since your only goal is to hire the absolute best, you'd only ever hire an interviewee if they're the best you've seen so far.  The basic tradeoff is this:

* If I hire them now, I risk the possibility that the best one would've come later.
* If I reject them now, I risk the possibility that they were actually the best.

The math is a bit tricky, but it turns out that the optimal decision rule is (approximately) to always reject the first 37% of candidates, then hire the first candidate afterwards who *ranks better than all the previous*.

The idea behind the solution is that it's too early to hire the first 37% you interview.  The probability that the best candidate is among the remaining applicants is still too high.  

### In popular media

The Secretary Problem has been used to describe search processes where you have to go through candidates one by one, like dating, house hunting, and job interviews.  It has achieved popular attention because of the seemingly ruthless rule of **automatically rejecting the first 37%**.  Especially when applied to dating, it would suggest that you should never marry your first few boyfriends/girlfriends, because *the probability that the best match is yet to come is still too high*.

### Critiques

The problem with applying this to real life is that some of the assumptions are unrealistic.  The worst culprit is `Unrealistic Assumption #3`.  The 37% rule is only optimal if you literally do not care about anything other than finding the *perfect match*.  The problem is set up in such a way that ending up with 2nd best is equally bad as ending up with the *worst candidate*.  There is no such scenario in real life where this is true, so the 37% rule is already not very applicable.

`Unrealistic Assumptions #1` and `#2` may be true in dating.  You often can't go back to a bf/gf that you've previously broken up with, and it's usually tough to explore multiple relationships at the same time.  However, in job interviews and house hunting, there are usually no such restrictions... there's just some risk that if you wait too long, the candidate is no longer available.  But that's a far cry from saying you have to immediately accept or reject a candidate after interviewing it.

One other thing I'll add is this.  The problem setup assumes you know what N is.  That is, you now exactly how many candidates there are going to be.  In most real life scenarios, like dating, you don't know that.  If you break up with your current partner, you don't know for sure another candidate is even going to arrive.

Oh, and one more unrealistic thing is that the information you get when you interview is purely *ordinal*, meaning it lets you *rank* the candidates, but it doesn't tell you an actual measure of the quality of *whether this person can do the job and how well*.  In most realistic settings, we care less about ranking amongst the candidates, and more about some absolute level of quality that we're looking for.

### Conclusion

It's a fun statistical puzzle, but the applicability to real life is way overstated.  One of those things where people hear a counterintuitive brutal strategy---"auTOmAtiCaLLy rEJECt thE FIrsT 37% oF APPLICanTs!"---and make much hay of it.... but yeah honestly you shouldn't do that in real life.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.
